analysis.one_liner: Raises the medical bar for asbestos lawsuits, caps damages, and bans punitive damages against asbestos companies.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced in April 2003, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the ground rules for asbestos lawsuits nationwide. It would have barred lawsuits for non-cancer asbestos conditions unless the claimant met strict medical criteria, imposed detailed evidence requirements for lung cancer and other cancer claims, capped pain-and-suffering awards at $250,000 (or $500,000 for mesothelioma), banned punitive damages, and limited each defendant to paying only its share of fault. It also would have restricted which doctors could certify claims and which courts plaintiffs could use. The bill never moved past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies facing asbestos lawsuits and their insurers would benefit most: fewer claims would survive the new medical screen, damage awards would be capped, punitive damages would disappear, and defendants would no longer be jointly liable for a full judgment. The bill's stated aim was also to preserve defendants' funds for the sickest claimants by deferring claims from people exposed but not yet impaired.

how_it_helps.text: It requires physical impairment as an essential element of any nonmalignant asbestos claim, with minimum criteria including a Class 2 or higher respiratory impairment rating and a diagnosis of asbestosis or diffuse pleural thickening, screening out claims from exposed-but-not-impaired people [S2].

It caps noneconomic (pain-and-suffering) damages at $250,000 or three times economic loss (whichever is greater), or $500,000 in mesothelioma cases, regardless of how many defendants are sued [S2, S3].

It bans punitive damages entirely and makes each defendant liable only for its own percentage of responsibility, ending joint liability under which a solvent defendant could pay the share of bankrupt ones [S2, S3].
It protects product sellers, renters, and lessors from liability unless the plaintiff proves negligent failure of care, breach of an independent express warranty, or intentional wrongdoing [S2, S3].
It lets defendants remove state-court cases to federal court if a state court declines to apply the bill's new consolidation, venue, and screening procedures [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: People sickened by asbestos exposure would bear the cost. Those with early-stage asbestosis or pleural disease, or cancers like lung or colon cancer that do not meet the bill's exposure-duration and documentation thresholds, could be turned away entirely. Everyone who did qualify would see pain-and-suffering awards capped and punitive damages eliminated, and would have to satisfy detailed testing and documentation requirements from a restricted pool of treating physicians.

drawbacks.text: The bill's minimum criteria for nonmalignant claims (a Class 2 respiratory impairment rating plus a diagnosis of asbestosis or diffuse pleural thickening with strict lung-function test results) are stricter than many state courts' standards, so people with documented exposure and real symptoms could be shut out of court [S2, S3].

Lung cancer claimants who smoked would need both radiological or pathological evidence of asbestosis AND specific occupational exposure durations, and exposure years before 1972 count fully while post-1979 exposure generally does not count at all, rules that exclude many workers with shorter or later exposures [S3].

A 'qualified physician' must be the claimant's treating doctor, earn little of his practice from litigation consulting, and be licensed and actively practicing in the state where the case is filed, which sharply limits which doctors can certify claims [S3].

The bill caps pain-and-suffering damages and eliminates punitive damages, which are the main tools for holding companies accountable when they concealed asbestos hazards, and the cap applies no matter how many defendants caused the harm [S2, S3].

The bill overrides state court procedures and venue rules, moving many cases to federal court and confining venue to the plaintiff's home state or the exposure state, removing choices that some plaintiffs' courts had allowed [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem the Supreme Court has called an 'elephantine mass' of over 200,000 pending cases, where claims from people exposed but not yet sick can drain money needed for the gravely ill, and more than 60 companies have gone bankrupt under the litigation weight [S2, S3]. But the remedy it chose was almost entirely defendant-side: it would not have created a compensation fund or guaranteed payment to anyone it screened out, it would have simply barred many claims and capped the rest, with punitive damages removed. Workers with serious but hard-to-document asbestos disease would have paid the price for the efficiencies gained by manufacturers and insurers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Cannon introduced the bill on April 3, 2003, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1, S5].
Nine House Republicans cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans [S4].
The action history shows no further activity after the referral: no committee markup, no report, no floor vote at any point in the 108th Congress [S5].
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with asbestos-related illness are better off, because the stricter medical screens, damage caps, and punitive-damages ban never took effect and their access to state and federal courts remains unchanged. Manufacturers and insurers seeking to cut their asbestos liabilities gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Chris Cannon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Asbestos Compensation Fairness Act of 2003 in the House.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred in the 108th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to die in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record; the sponsor and all 9 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrats are listed as supporters [S4].

industries.industry: Asbestos defendants (manufacturers, distributors, and building-product and industrial companies facing lawsuits)
industries.note: The bill would have screened out most claims from exposed-but-not-impaired people, capped pain-and-suffering awards, banned punitive damages, and replaced joint liability with proportional shares, sharply cutting what these companies pay. Ordinary sick workers would have absorbed the savings as denied and reduced claims.
Fewer and smaller claims mean smaller payouts on asbestos reserves. The bill's restrictions on eligible claimants and damages would have flowed directly to insurers' balance sheets.

industries.industry: Plaintiffs' trial lawyers handling asbestos cases
industries.note: Strict medical criteria, venue limits, removal to federal court, and damage caps would have shrunk the pool of viable claims and their fees. Here their interest ran alongside their sick clients' access to court.
